questions.prompt: How should an empty folder be identified?

options.label: By its explicit type, even when children is empty.
By having at least one child.
By a filename without a period.

questions.explanation: Files can have extensionless names and folders can be empty. The discriminated type is the structural contract, so child count and name heuristics are unreliable.

questions.prompt: Why are filenames unsuitable as the general key?

options.label: Different nodes can have the same filename.
React keys must be numeric.
A key must change whenever a folder opens.

questions.explanation: Stable unique IDs preserve identity even when names repeat or change. React accepts string keys; generating new keys on each toggle would reset component state.

questions.prompt: What happens to local child state when its conditional subtree unmounts?

options.label: It resets when the child is mounted again.
It is automatically saved forever by the parent.
It becomes a global variable.

questions.explanation: Removing the child from the rendered tree destroys its local state. A parent-owned expanded-ID set can retain the preference independently of child mounting.

questions.prompt: Why clone the expanded-ID Set before updating React state?

options.label: To produce a new state reference without mutating the previous set.
Because Sets cannot be changed at all.
To make lookup linear-time deliberately.

questions.explanation: A Set is mutable, but React state should be treated as read-only. Replacing it preserves previous snapshots and avoids relying on same-reference updates.

questions.prompt: What does an empty root array render?

options.label: A clear No files message.
An infinite recursive call.
A fabricated root folder.

questions.explanation: The brief asks for an empty state. Guarding the root list communicates that there is no data; inventing nodes changes the supplied filesystem.

options.label: No; nodes can be looked up by ID and their children rendered recursively.
Yes; a dictionary cannot represent hierarchy.
Yes; normalized data must be rendered as one flat string.

questions.explanation: Normalization separates storage from traversal. Child IDs preserve edges, and a recursive FileItem still follows those edges when expanded.

questions.prompt: Python recursion on an extremely deep tree may hit what limit?

options.label: The interpreter recursion limit.
The browser DOM limit.
A mandatory three-folder limit.

questions.explanation: Each recursive call uses stack depth. The practice fixture is finite and modest; a very deep or untrusted tree needs separate validation and traversal decisions.

questions.prompt: Put this baseline implementation recipe in dependency order. Each step prepares the next.

items.label: Test collapse ownership and hierarchy lines

questions.explanation: First establish the input and state contract, then implement the dependent transformation, and finally validate the observable result. Reversing these steps risks testing a UI whose rules or input identity have not been defined. This order is a rehearsal recipe, not the only possible engineering workflow.
